lines.4613: **The plan sampler comparison is DISCONFIRMED** (Table 207). In Table 207 the margin is the 5-point Hill-1 of plan noise minus that of the best text sampler. Plan noise matched or beat the best text sampler on 1 of the 5 decisive tasks, kth smallest (1.98 against 1.83 for enumerate and pick, P(plan noise at least best) 0.58, unresolved). On connected components, the shortest path task and two sum, base intent won (2.53, 1.45 and 1.61 against 1.09, 1.18 and 1.17), and on the grid task nothing moved much. The mean margin is -0.40 (95% interval -0.70 to -0.24), and only 1.8% of bootstrap replicates reach three wins. Every sensitivity keeps the verdict except one (Table 209): with the multistage samplers dropped (they were padded on the left), intent factored generation is the only text sampler left and plan noise beats it on 4 of 5 tasks, so the disconfirmation rests on base intent and on enumerate and pick. On the ten other tasks (Table 208) plan noise moved only cycle detection and first and last position, while text samplers moved substring search, find duplicate, Fibonacci, longest increasing subsequence, top-k frequent and first and last position. Two prompt knobs outside the text-sampler set also beat plan noise where it was strongest: the novelty instruction on kth smallest (2.03) and the semantic seed on the shortest path task (2.12).

lines.5503: We call a *full-state exchange* the replacement, in the forward pass of the neutral twin, of the residual states at a set of positions and blocks by the states the full ban prompt produces at the same positions; because the twin and the ban have identical token ids from the task text on, every task-specification position aligns. The exchanges covered four block bands at the task-specification positions (0 to 11, 12 to 23, 24 to 35, 0 to 35), a splice of the key-value cache of the condition span (the direct route), and the read position at all 36 blocks. The controls were the twin, a matched-norm random exchange (the state of the twin plus a fresh random direction scaled to the displacement that the ban itself causes per slot, block and position), a placebo that takes a second neutral twin as the source, and an identity exchange. The outcome is the share of correct programs implementing the substitute Y of the ban; the *transfer* of a cell is its Y share minus that of the twin, and its *recovery* is the transfer divided by that of the full ban. Each cell has N = 30 on paired slots. Tables 244 to 249 give every cell on the six tasks.
lines.5505: The prediction held where the route data said it should, and failed at one task where they said it should not. On shortest path, exchanging the full ban's task-specification states at all blocks into the twin turns 24 of 30 slots from Dijkstra to Bellman-Ford/SPFA (transfer 0.80, McNemar 24:0, Holm p 7e-7, pass ratio 0.90), while the condition-span splice and the read-position exchange transfer nothing. Blocks 12 to 23 alone carry 0.60 and blocks 24 to 35 alone 0.37; blocks 0 to 11 carry none. On kth smallest the same exchange transfers 0.57 to quickselect with every slot leaving the full sort, blocks 0 to 11 alone already transfer 0.40, and here the condition span also carries the ban (0.93). On connected components every slot leaves union find under the exchange at blocks 12 to 23 or 0 to 35 (off-default transfer 1.00), but only 0.37 to 0.47 land on the ban's BFS and the rest on DFS. On the grid task, whose route was carried by the prompt states in likelihood and mixed in behaviour, the exchange at all blocks transfers 0.47 toward DFS and the condition-span splice 0.33, so each carries part of the ban. On the direct-route tasks the condition-span splice alone reproduces the ban (two sum 1.00, find duplicate 0.90), as predicted, but on two sum the task-specification states also transfer brute force at 0.43, above the predicted ceiling of 0.2. The committed verdict is therefore not supported. The secondary predictions hold: the condition span carries at least 0.5 on the direct-route tasks and at most 0.2 on shortest path, the read position carries at most 0.2 everywhere (it carries 0.00 on all six tasks), the placebo moves at most 0.03, and the exchange beats the matched-norm random exchange where it transfers (shortest path 23:0, kth smallest 16:2, connected components 11:0). The ban's information, not the size of the perturbation, is what moves the algorithm.

lines.5623: The committed rule fitted a Firth logistic regression [125] of a correct off-default program on site indicators and the log displacements, so that sites are compared at matched downstream displacement (Tables 253 and 254). It returned the verdict withdrawn, for two reasons. The raw condition-span arm never reaches the plan site's downstream displacement, so it has no common support and its energy-matched arm stood in; and at alpha 8 every plan-site program failed (pass 0.00) while the read position began to move, which erases the read-position contrast in the preregistered model. A post-hoc sensitivity restricted to alpha of 4 or less (before breakage) puts the read position clearly below the plan site on both tasks: beta -3.76 (profile interval [-7.29, -0.47], cluster bootstrap [-8.18, -1.40]) on kth smallest and -4.98 ([-9.77, -0.89]; [-11.48, -1.53]) on connected components. The prefill-site claim is therefore withdrawn as preregistered, and its post-hoc form survives in bf16 at the ban-free unit.

Projected onto the plane of the first two principal components of the ten forced-prompt centroids (36% and 25% of their variance), the push leaves the forced-prompt manifold: already at alpha 1 it moves farther along the first component than the whole spread of the ten centroids. The prompt version of the top-five ban moves the task-specification states from below the centroid cloud into it, between the banned DFS and greedy best-first centroids and the three surviving centroids (bidirectional BFS and two variants of A*), and its behaviour stays inside the banned set (BFS 25, DFS 23 of 50; avoidance 0.00).

lines.5800: **The plan is a single-token fork.** Prefix resampling with change-point detection, the method of forking-path analyses [30, 31], located the fork: 24 base paths, 16 prefix lengths, 8 continuations each and a refinement, 3,712 continuations in all, scored by a partial-code labeller that agreed with the full labeller on 200 of 200 programs. Every one of 12 BFS base paths had a significant change point with a rise of at least 0.4, at prefix lengths 16 to 36. In 177 of 200 programs the first 32 tokens are identical (the code fence, `def solve(grid, start, goal):`, `rows = len(grid)`, `cols = len(grid[0])` and an indent), and the next token decides (Table 260): ` visited` leads to DFS (BFS probability 0.011 over 1,409 continuations), while a blank line, `if`, `queue` or `q` lead to BFS (0.95 to 1.00). The first token that identifies the algorithm in code comes a median of 138 tokens after the fork (10th to 90th percentile 80 to 181). The fork index was chosen by the token class with the most mutual information with the outcome (0.62 bits at index 32), after the first median rule landed on a deterministic indentation token; the change was made before the second commitment.
lines.5812: **Readable beyond the text, at the fork, but not specifically through the SAE.** Within one prompt, decodability before the first identifying token is at ceiling for every method, the visible-text control included (balanced accuracy 1.00 at all four layers), so the SAE has no advantage there; at the fork itself the test is undefined, because 185 of 200 samples share their prefix with a sample of the other class. Across prompts, the experiment built 120 neutral prompt variants by changing nouns and measured each variant's fork log-odds of BFS, which we write y (mean -0.92 nats, SD 0.67; the sampled BFS share tracks it at Spearman 0.65 over 60 variants of 10 samples). A Lasso on layer-29 SAE codes at the fork position predicts held-out y with R-squared 0.66, against 0.18 for a text-only model (difference 0.49, 95% interval 0.26 to 0.65, permutation p 0.003), above the difference-in-means readout (0.34) and a 16-component PCA of the raw residual (0.56) (Table 261). That meets the preregistered bar. Two checks outside the preregistration qualify it: a tuned ridge on the raw layer-29 residual reaches 0.72, and ridge on the same SAE codes reaches at most 0.09. The information is in the residual stream at the fork, and the SAE advantage depends on the estimator. At the task-specification positions, before any response token, the SAE codes do no better than the text (0.18).

lines.5837: **Steering: the features move the fork, difference in means moves it more, and every fork edit breaks programs.** We call an *SAE clamp* setting the k latents that best separate forced-BFS from forced-DFS prompts (input-selected) to their BFS-class mean at the fork position; output-scored latents are chosen instead by their attribution to the fork's logit difference, and the two sets of 20 share 2 latents. At the fork position of layer 22, edits at matched norm moved y by +4.04 nats for the difference-in-means direction, +1.78 for the SAE clamp of the top 20 input-selected latents, +0.51 for 20 random latents and +0.12 for an isotropic direction. Table 261b gives the whole dose-response sweep over the 120 prompt variants (11,280 measurements), at the fork and at the task-specification positions. In generation (N = 50 paired slots), the twin wrote BFS in 13 programs; the SAE clamp raised this to 30 (top 20 latents) and 36 (top 50), the difference-in-means edit at the same norm to 46 and 49, and random latents to 21 (Table 262). Every edit at the fork lowered the pass rate, from 0.84 for the twin to 0.58 and 0.48 for the SAE clamps and 0.32 and 0.16 for difference in means, so the preregistered outcome, correct BFS programs, shows no significant effect anywhere after Holm correction, and no feature claim is made. The preregistered feature rule (SAE target-correct count at least the difference-in-means count, at a pass rate of at least 0.8 times the twin's) is also met by random latents at k = 50 (9 against 7, pass 0.76), so it cannot discriminate here. The informative comparisons are on attempted BFS, and they are descriptive: the SAE clamp beats the twin (17:0 and 23:0 discordant slots, p 1.5e-5 and 2.4e-7) and random latents (15:0, p 6.1e-5), and difference in means beats the SAE clamp at matched norm (16:0, p 3.1e-5). At matched effect on y rather than matched norm, difference in means and the SAE clamp shift the plan equally (32 against 30 BFS, p 0.50; 34 against 36, p 0.63) and difference in means keeps slightly more programs correct (13 against 9, 14 against 10). Edits at the task-specification positions do nothing (12 to 19 BFS against 13). Steering toward DFS works cleanly for both (SAE 47 of 50, difference in means 50 of 50, against 37 for the twin; pass 0.98 to 1.00). Difference-in-means steering of a code model's choice of language and library has shown the same trade-off, with overly strong interventions reducing output quality [130]. AxBench found simple baselines ahead of SAE steering [34], and a 2026 reanalysis puts SAEs close to AxBench's reference when latents are selected and labelled by a supervised pipeline [131]; here, at comparable norms, neither the input-selected nor the output-scored clamp reached the difference-in-means edit (Table 261b).
lines.5889: **DAS finds the choice in one direction at the fork, and forcing it breaks the program.** DAS at the fork position of layer 22, with forced-BFS prompts as sources, moved held-out y by +8.8, +9.5 and +9.8 nats at ranks 1, 2 and 4, against -0.08 to +0.05 for random subspaces of the same rank (Table 263). The shuffled-source control was uninformative as built, because every source was a forced-BFS prompt. In generation the rank-4 interchange made 50 of 50 programs BFS and 0 of 50 passed. Together with the difference-in-means result, this says that the plan is close to one direction at one position, and that pushing it hard costs correctness, as subspace interventions can when they leave the model's natural range [122].

lines.5911: **The top-five prohibition in a model that writes two algorithms.** Banning the five most common grid algorithms (BFS, DFS, IDDFS, A* and greedy best-first, which share one catalogue label here) left no program outside the banned set: avoidance 0.00, as in Qwen3-8B in iteration 2 (Table 265). The ban pushed Gemma from its default DFS to BFS (10 to 41 of 50; McNemar 32:1, p 7.9e-9) and cut the pass rate from 0.86 to 0.38. In actual activation coordinates (PCA, Isomap with k = 10 and classical MDS of layers 17 and 22, raw and SAE codes), the top-five prompt states sit next to the banned A* and greedy cluster (Table 266); among all 15 ways of splitting the six catalogue centroids into four banned and two survivors, the observed split ranks first in three of the four spaces (rank share 0.067) and third in the fourth (0.20). The prohibition lands inside the banned region, not at its edge or on the opposite side. The single-name bans of BFS and DFS left the banned algorithm in 11 and 8 of 50 programs, and the forced prompts gave BFS 50 of 50 (38 correct) and DFS 50 of 50 (45 correct).

lines.5962: **The NLA never names the planned algorithm before the code.** Two blind judges from different families (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite and Mistral Small 3.2, both scoring 1.00 on calibration; a third model resolved 1,064 disagreements) mapped each of 6,180 explanations to a catalogue algorithm or to none named (Table 269). Every preregistered readout at the end-of-prompt positions is exactly zero (Table 270). On ban prompts, explanations named the substitute in 0 of 16 states (only two sum had a substitute, so this test is underpowered); on twin prompts they named the default in 0 of 112, as did the text-only reader; on ban failures they named the default the model still writes in 0 of 96. The positive control failed too: on forced `Implement Y` prompts the explanations called Y planned in 0 of 7 tasks, while the text-only reader did so on all of them, and they mentioned the algorithm named in the prompt in 0.7% of cases. The explanations describe the local format line, such as a request for no explanation or a Python code block to follow, and confabulate the task (Fibonacci, medians, prime numbers); 4,733 of 5,700 judged explanations name no algorithm at all. At generated tokens the NLA sometimes names the realised algorithm before the visible text identifies it (up to 0.28 at token 8 under the ban), but an outside reader who sees only the prompt and prefix predicts the realised algorithm better, per sample (0.25 against 0.07; exact McNemar 20:88, p 2e-11).

examples.input: **Steering: the features move the fork, difference in means moves it more, and every fork edit breaks programs.** We call an *SAE clamp* setting the k latents that best separate forced-BFS from forced-DFS prompts (input-selected) to their BFS-class mean at the fork position; output-scored latents are chosen instead by their attribution to the fork's logit difference, and the two sets of 20 share 2 latents. At the fork position of layer 22, edits at matched norm moved y by +4.04 nats for the difference-in-means direction, +1.78 for the SAE clamp of the top 20 input-selected latents, +0.51 for 20 random latents and +0.12 for an isotropic direction. Table 261b gives the whole dose-response sweep over the 120 prompt variants (11,280 measurements), at the fork and at the task-specification positions. In generation (N = 50 paired slots), the twin wrote BFS in 13 programs; the SAE clamp raised this to 30 (top 20 latents) and 36 (top 50), the difference-in-means edit at the same norm to 46 and 49, and random latents to 21 (Table 262). Every edit at the fork lowered the pass rate, from 0.84 for the twin to 0.58 and 0.48 for the SAE clamps and 0.32 and 0.16 for difference in means, so the preregistered outcome, correct BFS programs, shows no significant effect anywhere after Holm correction, and no feature claim is made. The preregistered feature rule (SAE target-correct count at least the difference-in-means count, at a pass rate of at least 0.8 times the twin's) is also met by random latents at k = 50 (9 against 7, pass 0.76), so it cannot discriminate here. Edits at the task-specification positions do nothing (12 to 19 BFS against 13). examples.input: Priced as a knob, plan noise is not the practical answer on the evidence so far. Under the 8-bit engine at the ban unit it was the cheapest route to a second correct algorithm on kth smallest (Hill-1 2.72 within 5 pass points) and connected components (2.09); fixed random directions reached above 2 at no cost on kth smallest and two sum, but as maxima over 21 and 9 directions. Against text-level plan samplers, measured in bf16 at the ban-free unit where plan noise was weak, plan noise matched the best sampler on 1 of 5 decisive tasks: an intent sentence written by the base model, with the code written by the instruct model, won on connected components, the shortest path task and two sum (2.53, 1.45 and 1.61), and enumerate and pick reached the most raw diversity at 16 to 62 pass points. That comparison has not been repeated at the absolute unit at which plan noise is strong. Plan noise beat decoding at matched departure on kth smallest at alpha 2 (13:0) and not elsewhere (6:3). Generate then select [43] and enumerate and pick, which hand the choice to an external random draw, remain ceilings with large pass costs.

examples.input: What decides the replacement under a modal ban has measured leads and no confirmed rule. The likelihood instrument of iteration 2 cannot decide it, and substitution by the alternative the model states is not supported in Qwen3-8B. The runner-up of the base model names where a push lands in 17 of 21 recorded events across Qwen3-8B and Gemma (5 of 5 on the 8-bit screen, 1 of 2 on the bf16 remeasurement, 3 of 3 and 3 of 4 on new tasks, 5 of 7 in Gemma), and it beats the instruct twin's teacher-forced ranking of algorithm openings 8:1 where the two disagree (p 0.020, retrospective). But where the instruct twin already writes an alternative, that alternative names the landing as often (6 of 7), and on the 8 held-out events where the twin wrote none the base runner-up named 5 (p 0.053): the landing half is descriptive. The base model's own variety does not say whether a task can be moved: over 13 new units its off-default share ranks movability at Spearman 0.15 (95% interval -0.44 to 0.65; power 0.63 at a true 0.6; 0.035 if count inversions' share is taken from its correct programs), so a strong relation is excluded and a moderate one is not; only the runtime merit of the fastest alternative tracks movability after Holm correction (0.71). Both verdicts are conditional on the ban-free unit and seeds of iteration 5. Writing the task-specification states of the base model into the instruct prefill reopened the base runner-up on 1 of 5 Qwen3-8B tasks and 2 of 7 Gemma tasks, the latter where the instruct twin already wrote it 8% to 12% of the time.
